edges.description: Under the T-cell model, food-specific T-cell activation drives intestinal inflammation and permeability; human data supporting a causal role are limited and contested.
Innate effector cells, together with locally produced TNF-alpha, are proposed to drive mucosal inflammation and loss of barrier function; the sequence has not been demonstrated directly in FPIES.
FPIES reactions activate neuroendocrine as well as innate pathways; how the immune reaction recruits the serotonergic emetic reflex is not established; purinergic signaling is one candidate.

nodes.description: Cow's milk protein, usually given as cow's milk-based infant formula, is the most common FPIES trigger in infancy and the main trigger of chronic FPIES. The caseins dominate the milk antigen response in IgE-mediated milk allergy, and they are the milk antigen most studied in FPIES, where casein-specific antibody and regulatory T-cell responses are deficient; whether casein or whey proteins are the operative FPIES antigens has not been resolved.

nodes.description: Children with cow's milk FPIES mount weak or absent humoral responses to milk proteins, with low casein-specific IgG, IgG4 and IgA, and their casein-stimulated T cells show deficient TGF-beta and low IL-10 production. These deficits distinguish active from resolved or tolerant states and are proposed to reflect failed oral tolerance to milk proteins, but whether they cause reactions or merely mark active disease is not established.

nodes.description: Serotonin released by enterochromaffin cells can activate vagal afferents and trigger the vomiting reflex. The efficacy of the 5-HT3 receptor antagonist ondansetron in suppressing FPIES vomiting is the main support for a serotonergic emetic step; the serotonin metabolite 5-hydroxyindoleacetate rises in serum after symptomatic reactions.

nodes.description: T cells responsive to the trigger food (milk, soy or rice) are more frequent in active than in resolved FPIES, and casein stimulation elicits CD4+ T-cell proliferation with Th2 cytokines in cow's milk FPIES. Because similar responses occur in tolerant or IgE-allergic controls, these cells may track disease activity without being the effector mechanism. Pan-T-cell activation and redistribution from the circulation follow a positive challenge.

nodes.description: Food-antigen exposure is believed to cause intestinal inflammation with increased permeability and fluid shift into the intestinal lumen. Early biopsy studies of milk-exposed infants showed altered intestinal architecture, mucosal TNF-alpha expression, and inflammatory cells in fecal mucus after challenge.

nodes.description: Positive food challenges in active FPIES are followed by profound activation of circulating monocytes, neutrophils, natural killer cells and eosinophils, with transcriptional innate signatures and rises in serum IL-8 and IL-10, absent in children who have outgrown FPIES. Symptomatic reactions also carry an IL-17 family signature (IL-17A, IL-22, CCL20), with preferential activation of non-conventional T-cell populations.

evidence.reference_title: Acute FPIES reactions are associated with an IL-17 inflammatory signature.
evidence.snippet: Symptomatic FPIES challenge results were associated with significant elevation of levels of cytokines and chemokines, including IL-17 family markers (IL-17A, IL-22, IL-17C, and CCL20) and T-cell activation (IL-2), and innate inflammatory markers (IL-8, oncostatin M, leukemia inhibitory factor, TNF-α, IL-10, and IL-6).

evidence.reference_title: Systemic innate immune activation in food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Profiling of whole blood by CyTOF demonstrated profound activation of cells of the innate immune system after food challenge, including monocytes, neutrophils, natural killer cells, and eosinophils. Activation was not observed in children with outgrown FPIES.

nodes.description: Strict elimination of the trigger food, with dietetic support, regular growth monitoring and a written emergency plan; maternal dietary elimination is not recommended for a thriving, asymptomatic breastfed infant.

evidence.snippet: Management relies of avoidance of food triggers, treatment of accidental exposures, and periodic re-evaluations with supervised oral food challenges to monitor for resolution.
